The value will manifest once production stabilizes, airline demand returns, and the franchise's long-term utility as a duopolist is realized over its $463 billion backlog [D01].

final.memo:
We have looked at the Company and have decided to pass. While the business occupies a critical position in a global duopoly for large-commercial-aircraft manufacturing, its current financial state is precarious [D01]. We only invest in businesses we can understand, and today the company's financial results—swinging to a $636 million net loss and suffering from negative free cash flow—render any estimate of intrinsic value pure speculation [D01], [D02].

We prioritize durable competitive advantages and the ability to generate consistent returns on capital, yet the company is currently burdened by $27.3 billion in debt and $4 billion in abnormal production costs [D01]. A business that requires constant external validation of its solvency does not fit our definition of a wonderful business [D01], [D05]. Even with a $463 billion backlog, the immediate threats posed by the collapse in airline finances and unresolved safety-certification issues create an environment where permanent loss of capital is a very real possibility [D01], [D05].

In our view, this is a situation better described as a gamble than an investment. We have $128 billion in cash and Treasury bills that can be put to work in ways that do not risk Berkshire's reputation or capital [D08]. We prefer to own businesses that thrive in almost any economic climate, rather than those that require a perfect recovery to avoid bankruptcy or catastrophic dilution [D05], [D08]. Just as a ship in a storm should seek a harbor, we find it prudent to remain in our cash position until a truly compelling, high-quality opportunity appears.
